claims.text: Prolonged thermal exposure activates diffusion-mediated nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates from an initially metastable solid solution.
Fine, uniformly distributed Mg-rich precipitates promote formation of a continuous protective oxide scale.
A continuous protective oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Fine Mg-rich precipitates help retain corrosion resistance.
Coarse or grain-boundary-segregated intermetallics disrupt oxide-scale continuity and accelerate localized degradation.
The initial material is a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution microstructure.
Annealing at 850–1050 °C for varying durations will induce phase separation.
Annealing will produce Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates both within the matrix and at grain boundaries.
Decomposition of the metastable solid solution proceeds by diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth.
Intermetallic formation changes local chemistry and microstructural interfaces.
Changes in local chemistry and interfaces modulate the adhesion and continuity of oxide layers formed during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
Thermally treated samples will develop a two-phase microstructure containing uniformly dispersed fine intermetallic precipitates.
An optimal precipitate size and distribution will produce a more continuous alumina- or chromia-based protective scale.
Coarse or grain-boundary-concentrated intermetallics will cause faster corrosion and oxidation than in the pristine metastable state.
The as-cast state is a homogeneous metastable solid solution lacking stabilized intermetallic phases.
The absence of stabilized intermetallic phases gives the as-cast state relatively lower intrinsic oxide protection.
Prolonged exposure at 850–1050 °C in oxidizing environments is a relevant regime for evaluating high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Intermetallic-precipitation kinetics become significant within the stated 850–1050 °C service regime.
